strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in the literature: prior work (Nelson et al., 2022) simplifies the reward model by making it depend on beliefs rather than actual hidden states, and this paper convincingly explains why this substitution is not innocuous (Section 3, Appendix B), showing the loss of the reduction to linear contextual bandits.

The technical contribution is substantial: the paper carefully identifies why standard LinUCB/martingale arguments fail when rewards depend directly on unobserved states (the z_t/d_t terms are not measurable w.r.t. any natural filtration that also makes a_t measurable), and resolves this via a staged algorithm combined with an L^2-Markov argument leveraging HMM forgetting properties.

Provides genuinely high-probability regret bounds (not just in-expectation, as in Nelson et al.) that are also reward-model-free (no dependence on reward gaps), which is a meaningful improvement in guarantee quality.

The paper is careful and rigorous about a subtle but important technical issue in HMM parameter estimation: label/permutation ambiguity across rounds, and provides an explicit alignment procedure with a full consistency proof (Appendix C.2) — this is often glossed over in related literature.

Good scholarly positioning: the related-work discussion clearly differentiates from Azizzadenesheli et al., Zhou et al., Hong et al., Galozy et al., and offers a fairly complete, point-by-point comparison to Nelson et al. (2022), including re-deriving their result more directly and highlighting exactly where each assumption/relaxation matters.
The special case (single-round stages) recovers a generalized, more direct treatment of the Nelson et al. model with an improved/simplified proof technique.
weaknesses: No empirical evaluation whatsoever: Appendix F explicitly states numerical simulations are deferred to 'a version 2 of this article.' For a paper proposing a concrete algorithm (Box A/B) with complex confidence bonuses, the absence of any experiments (even small-scale synthetic ones) is a significant weakness that limits confidence in practical performance and correctness of the implementation.

The main T^{7/8} regret bound is substantially weaker than typical sqrt(T) bandit rates or even the T^{3/4} rate in the simplified model, and no lower bound or hardness result is given to establish whether this rate (or the T^{3/4} rate) is unavoidable; the authors acknowledge this as fully open, which tempers the significance of the contribution.

The belief-estimation guarantee (Assumption 4.1, instantiated via Lemma 4.3) requires a fairly restrictive class of HMMs (Assumption 4.2: finite context space, full column rank emission matrix, invertible transition matrix with strictly positive entries, stationary initial distribution) — this substantially limits the scope of applicability relative to the generality suggested by the main text.
The algorithm requires knowledge of the horizon T to set λ and stage length ℓ optimally (Theorem 5.2), i.e., it is not anytime; no discussion of standard doubling-trick extensions is provided.

The confidence bonuses and constants (e.g., f_t in Theorem 5.2) are extremely complex, and the polynomial (1/√δ) dependence on the confidence parameter from the L^2-Markov argument (versus the usual √ln(1/δ) from martingale/sub-Gaussian arguments) suggests the bounds may be quite loose in practice, which is not investigated.

The presentation, while thorough, is very dense and heavily front-loads intuition into lengthy appendices (over 30 pages), making the main text's claims (e.g., the T^{7/8} rate, the role of γ, ℓ, λ) difficult to fully verify without extensive cross-referencing; a more self-contained proof sketch with clearer intermediate quantities in the main text would improve accessibility.

The comparison to Nelson et al. in Section 5.1 partly rests on adopting a stronger sub-Gaussian noise assumption (Assumption 2.2 vs. 2.3) to bypass their forgetting-based analysis; while acknowledged, this makes the 'more direct and simpler' claim somewhat assumption-dependent rather than a strict improvement under identical conditions.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap in Nelson et al. (2022): the belief-dependent (rather than state-dependent) reward model is a substantive simplification, and the authors give a clear, convincing argument (Section 3.1) for why this reduction to linear contextual bandits breaks down once rewards depend directly on the hidden state.

The technical machinery is detailed and appears carefully worked out: the staged LinUCB strategy, the introduction of the intermediate filtration U_t, the L^2-Markov argument adapted from Nelson et al. to control the non-martingale term S^Δ, and the extension of the elliptic potential lemma to staged updates (Lemma E.6) are all nontrivial technical contributions with complete, transparent proofs in the appendix.

The paper improves on Nelson et al. (2022) along multiple genuine axes for the simplified model: high-probability (not just expectation) bounds, no reliance on reward gaps, and no non-degeneracy/coverage assumption on the design matrix.

The treatment of belief estimation (spectral method + alignment step for label consistency + Bayes filtering) is thorough and self-contained, addressing a real practical difficulty (permutation ambiguity of hidden-state labels) that prior works glossed over.

The discussion sections (3, 4.1, 6) are unusually candid about where the technique is loose (e.g., the L^2-Markov vs. martingale argument, the open question of optimality), which is commendable scientific honesty.
weaknesses: There are no experiments whatsoever: Appendix F literally states "Numerical simulations will be provided in a version 2 of this article." For a paper proposing new algorithms (Box A, Box B) this is a serious gap -- there is no empirical evidence that the proposed staged strategy behaves reasonably, that the belief-estimation/alignment procedure is practically stable, or that the T^{7/8} and T^{3/4} rates are not wildly pessimistic in practice. Submitting with a promise of a future version undermines reviewability of the actual contribution.

The headline regret rate for the main (and most novel) contribution is T^{7/8}, which is a weak, and arguably not very useful, guarantee for large/moderate T; the paper itself acknowledges this may not be optimal and leaves closing the gap to T^{3/4} as open. This makes the practical significance of Theorem 5.2 questionable.

The analysis rests on a fairly strong and specific set of assumptions (Assumption 4.2: finite context space, full column-rank emission matrix, invertible transition matrix with strictly positive entries, stationary initial distribution) needed to invoke the particular spectral-method guarantee (Lemma 4.3); generalization to continuous contexts is only sketched via a pointer to prior work, not analyzed.

The comparison to Nelson et al. (2022) is somewhat uneven: the authors' own "improved" analysis of the *simplified* model (Appendix A, Theorem A.1) requires strengthening the noise assumption to full sub-Gaussianity (Assumption 2.2) rather than the second-moment assumption Nelson et al. use; the paper argues this relaxation is "unimportant," but this is asserted rather than rigorously justified, and it somewhat undercuts the claimed superiority of the new analysis.

The confidence-bonus expressions (e.g., in Theorem 5.2) and intermediate quantities (T_{B,M,ν}, multiple layers of constants C0..C3, L0..L2) are extremely complex and not reduced to an interpretable closed form; this heavily hampers reproducibility and makes it difficult for a reader to assess tightness or practical magnitude of the bounds.

The core novel technical device (the stage-wise filtration U_t plus L^2-Markov control of S^Δ) is explicitly presented as borrowed/adapted from Nelson et al. (2022)'s proof technique (Appendix B), so the degree of original methodological novelty, as opposed to careful but incremental extension, is more limited than the framing in the introduction ("Direct Approach", "Contribution 1/2") suggests.

The writing is extremely dense and notation-heavy even for a theory paper, with the main text deferring almost all substantive content (algorithms, proofs, even the belief-estimation subroutine) to a 43-page appendix; the 10-page main body mostly previews results without allowing independent verification, limiting accessibility and reviewability within the page limit.

The significance of the contribution is somewhat narrow: it resolves a specific technical gap in one prior paper's model rather than demonstrating broader applicability (e.g., to richer reward models, non-linear rewards, or real-world latent-state bandit applications), and absent experiments, it is hard to gauge whether the state-dependent model meaningfully changes practical performance relative to the belief-dependent simplification.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely more natural and more difficult model than Nelson et al. (2022): rewards depend directly on the hidden state rather than on the belief, which breaks the reduction to linear contextual bandits that prior work relied upon. This is a meaningful conceptual contribution clearly explained in Section 3.

The identification of the three key quantities to control (S^diff, S^belief, S^eta) and the extension of the L2-Markov argument from Nelson et al. (2022) to handle the non-martingale term S^diff arising from direct state-dependence is a real technical contribution, carefully executed in Appendix E.

The treatment is thorough and self-contained: belief estimation guarantees (Assumption 4.1, Lemma 4.3) are derived from first principles by combining spectral HMM estimation with an explicit, non-trivial state-labeling alignment procedure (Appendix C.2), which is often glossed over in related literature.
The extension of the elliptic potential lemma to staged/frozen Gram matrices (Lemma E.6) is a clean and useful technical tool that could be reused in other staged-bandit analyses.

The comparison to Nelson et al. (2022) is detailed and mostly fair: the paper is explicit about which improvements come from strengthening noise assumptions (sub-Gaussian vs. second moment) versus from genuinely new techniques, and acknowledges where its own bound is weaker (looser rate, no coverage-assumption removal trade-off is honestly discussed).
weaknesses: No experiments are provided at all; the paper explicitly states numerical simulations are deferred to 'a version 2 of this article' (Appendix F). For a paper proposing new algorithms (staged LinUCB with belief estimation) this is a significant gap—there is no empirical validation that the method works, that the stage length/parameter choices are practical, or that the belief-alignment procedure functions robustly in finite samples. Submitting without experiments to a venue like ICML is a substantial weakness.

The headline regret rate achieved, T^{7/8}, is quite weak compared to the canonical sqrt(T) rate for linear bandits, and even weaker than the T^{3/4} rate for the simplified model. The paper's own limitations section admits this may not be tight and that closing the gap to T^{3/4} is open. This tempers the significance of the contribution: the 'direct' model is solved only in a loose, far-from-optimal sense.

The reliance on an L2-Markov/Chebyshev-type argument (rather than exponential martingale concentration) yields 1/sqrt(delta) rather than sqrt(log(1/delta)) dependence on confidence, which is a known source of looseness; the paper is transparent about this but does not explore alternative, potentially sharper proof techniques beyond noting it as future work.

The belief estimation machinery (Assumption 4.1, spectral method guarantees) requires restrictive assumptions (Assumption 4.2: finite context space, full column rank emission matrix, invertible transition matrix with strictly positive minimum entries, stationary initial distribution) that substantially restrict the class of HMMs covered, despite being described as a 'wide class.' The extension to continuous contexts (Example 2) is only sketched by pointer to prior work, not integrated into the main theorem.

The staging mechanism, while necessary for the proof, creates a strategy that only updates its reward-parameter estimates at coarse stage boundaries (length ~T^{3/4}), which is a strong departure from the fully sequential nature of typical contextual bandit algorithms and likely hurts practical performance substantially, something that could only be verified with the (currently missing) experiments.

The comparison of pseudo-regret vs. actual regret is relegated to a brief remark (Remark 2.4) without full proof details, leaving the practical interpretation of the guarantees (whether they bound true accumulated reward loss) somewhat incomplete in the main text.

The writing, while generally careful, is dense and occasionally rough (e.g., minor typos like 'partiel elements', inconsistent notation switches between b̄_t and b_t across appendices), which may hinder reproducibility/verification by readers not deeply steeped in this specific niche of HMM-bandit literature.
